newsitem.title: USA: Financial mess latest stain on Miami's tarnished image.
newsitem.headline: Financial mess latest stain on Miami's tarnished image.

text.p: Miami's financial mess is just the latest blow to the esteem of a city that is as grimy on the inside as it is glamorous on the outside.

The money crisis topped by a $68 million budget deficit forced Florida Governor Lawton Chiles on Tuesday to declare a financial emergency. He will appoint a panel to oversee the city's recovery from the crippling mismanagement.
Two ratings services have dropped Miami's bond rating to make it a "junk city".

The dubious accolade was the last thing needed by a city plagued by a corruption scandal in city hall, tourist murders and one of the worst crime rates in the United States, racial tensions and severe economic inequalities.
Ordinary citzens reacting to the crisis said they felt embarrassed.
"It's one thing after another down here," said Rafael Serpa, owner of the Brickell Grill, a popular lunchtime spot in Miami's financial district. "It's kind of scary."
"It's a beautiful city but it's always been very corrupt. Maybe now we'll see a change in the way of doing business."

One commentator said the sorry events made Miami look like a banana republic -- a stinging irony in a city that is a hub of trade and business for Latin America, itself for years mired in corruption and inefficiency.

"It seems like there is absolutely no systems of checks and balances. So this is very much operating like small town politics in a Third World nation," said Jerry Haar of the University of Miami North-South Centre.

The grim assesment contrasts with the other view of Miami -- a dynamic business centre, a culturally diverse and trendy city offering plenty of fun in the sun, and a playground of the young, rich and famous.
Tourist officials were concerned that although the financial crisis specifically concerned only the City of Miami, other parts of the metropolis would be smeared.
Although the Miami urban area has over two million residents in more than two dozen cities, only 365,000 live within Miami city limits.
Mayco Villafana, Greater Miami Convention and Visitors Bureau spokesman, said the problem did not affect business and leisure visitors but it would harm perceptions.
"They will not see the difference between the city of Miami with the entire area. We anticipate we may have to answer many questions," he said."
The financial mess follows a corruption scandal in city hall which rammed home to citizens how deep the rot went.
City Commissioner Miller Dawkins pleaded guilty in October to accepting bribes for contracts. He faces 15 years in jail and $500 million in fines.
City Manager Cesar Odio, a hero to Miami's vast Cuban immigrant community, is awaitung trial on similar charges.
Miami's crime is already legendary. A string of murders and muggings of tourists attracted international attention.

Last month Money magazine rated it one of the most dangerous cities in the United States, ranking 196 out of 202 surveyed. Residents queried listed burglary, car theft, robbery, assault, rape and murder as constant worries.

As some citizens watched news of the rescue plan on Tuesday evening, in the poor immigrant community of Little Haiti, gunmen in a pick-up fired into a crowd outside a food store. One person was killed and four wounded, police said. They did not know the reason for the shooting.

"The real crisis that Miami faces, it's a multiple crisis," Haar said. "One of the principal problems is that Miami believes it's own press releases but the labour force is unskilled, there are public safety problems."
The city has failed to provide decent education and jobs for the poor, he said.
"The underclass is locked in without any possibility of pulling its bootstraps. In this community, the sum equals less than its parts."
